title: Aquarium Setup: "Golden Rules" and the Nitrogen Cycle
content:
Aquarium setup is the most important and difficult stage. Mistakes at this stage almost always lead to the death of fish.

## What is the Nitrogen Cycle?
The Nitrogen Cycle is a natural biological process that occurs in the aquarium and converts toxic waste into relatively safe substances. Without this process, your aquarium is just a tank of poisonous water.

*Stages:* Fish excrete *Ammonia (NH3)* → Bacteria → *Nitrites (NO2)* → Bacteria → *Nitrates (NO3)*.
*Danger:* Ammonia and Nitrites are extremely toxic to fish, even in small concentrations. Nitrates are less dangerous but need to be removed regularly.

## "Golden Rules" for Aquarium Cycling (Fishless Cycle)
To establish a colony of beneficial bacteria, you must run the cycle without live fish.
*Preparation:* Install equipment (filter, heater), substrate, decorations. Add water, include a *conditioner (dechlorinator)* to neutralize chlorine.
*Cycling:* Introduce an ammonia source (you can buy special starter bacteria or use a little food). Turn on the filter and heater.
*Testing — The Critical Step:* Use *water tests* (liquid dropper tests, not strips!) to monitor NH3, NO2, and NO3.
*Waiting:* The process takes *3-6 weeks*. Do not introduce fish until tests show 0 ammonia (NH3) and 0 nitrites (NO2).
*Fish:* Introduce fish gradually (2-3 specimens per week) so the biofilter can adapt to the growing load.

title: Symptoms of "Ammonia/Nitrite Poisoning"
content:
If you see these signs, check your water parameters immediately!

*Ammonia (NH3):* Fish gasp for air at the surface; their gills are bright red or purple.
*Nitrites (NO2):* Fish may also gasp, lay on the bottom, and breathe heavily. The water may look clear.

## Emergency Aid:
*Immediate Water Change:* Perform a *25–50%* water change (be sure to add dechlorinator!). This will lower the concentration of toxins.
*Increase Aeration:* Turn the air pump to full power to increase oxygen content.
*Do not feed:* Do not feed the fish for 24 hours to reduce the production of new waste.

**Conclusion:** Water tests are your main tool. Do not buy fish on the same day as the aquarium. Successful cycling requires patience.

title: Equipment: Filter, Heater
content:
Properly selected and functioning equipment keeps the aquarium environment stable. Equipment failure can quickly lead to disaster.

## How to Choose a Filter and Heater
*Filter: The Heart of the Aquarium*
The filter performs three functions: *mechanical* (removes debris), *chemical* (removes toxins), and *biological* (houses beneficial nitrogen cycle bacteria — this is its main task!).

*How to choose:* The filter's power should process the entire volume of water in the aquarium at least *3–4 times per hour*. For example, a 100-liter aquarium needs a filter with a flow rate of 300–400 L/h.
*Types:* *Internal* (for small aquariums, simple) or *external (canister)* (for large volumes, provides better biological filtration).
*Maintenance:* *Never rinse filter sponges with tap water!* Chlorine will kill beneficial bacteria. Rinse them in water removed from the aquarium during a water change.

*Heater: Temperature Stability*
*How to choose:* Power is calculated by the formula *0.5–1 Watt per liter* of water. A 75–100 W heater is suitable for a 100-liter aquarium.
*Important:* Install a thermometer (not the one built into the heater) to monitor the actual temperature. *Sudden temperature spikes* (even 2–3°C) cause stress and disease in fish.

title: Emergency Aeration
content:
Oxygen enters the water not only through the air pump but also through the water surface. A sudden failure of the air pump or filter (which also creates water movement) can cause oxygen deprivation (especially at night).

*Symptoms of Oxygen Deprivation:*
*Fish gather at the surface,* gulping air.
*Fish breathe heavily;* their gill covers move rapidly.

## Emergency Aeration (Until You Get a New Air Pump):
*Lower the temperature:* Cooler water retains oxygen better. Gradually cool the water by 1–2 degrees.
*Increase surface area contact:* Use a ladle or cup to scoop water from the aquarium and pour it back from a slight height. This breaks the surface and actively saturates the water with oxygen. Do this regularly until aeration is restored.
*Do not feed the fish:* Digestion consumes a lot of oxygen.

**Conclusion:** Regular inspection and cleaning of equipment are mandatory. In case of failure, emergency water stirring will help the fish survive until repair or replacement.

title: Compatibility
content:
The most common beginner mistake is placing fish with completely different needs or temperaments in one aquarium. An ideal aquarium is a world where all inhabitants feel safe.

## Golden Rules of Compatibility
Before buying a new fish, check three main factors:
*Size (Predation):* If a fish fits into another fish's mouth, it will be eaten. You absolutely cannot keep large predatory fish (e.g., aggressive cichlids) with small peaceful fish (e.g., Neons).
*Temperature and Water Parameters:* You cannot mix fish that require warm water (Discus, 28-30°C) with those that require cool water (Goldfish, 20-22°C). The same hardness and acidity (pH) are also important.
*Temperament (Aggression):* You cannot house aggressive and boisterous fish with slow-moving or veil-tailed (long-tailed) species.

## Who Can and Who Absolutely Cannot Be Kept Together:
*Peaceful schooling fish (Neons, Tetras, Rasboras.)* - *Cannot be kept alone* (they will die from stress). *Cannot be kept with Barbs* (fins will be nipped) and *Angelfish* (they might be eaten).
*Veil-tailed and slow-moving fish (Goldfish (some breeds), Male Bettas.)* - *Cannot be kept with Barbs* or *Bagrid Catfish* — their long fins will be nipped or damaged.
*Semi-aggressive fish (Angelfish, Barbs, some small Cichlids.)* - Angelfish can become predators to small Neons as they grow. Barbs are known as "fin-nippers."
*Aggressive fish (Large Cichlids (Oscar, Acaras), some Catfish.)* - *Strictly forbidden* to house with peaceful and small species. They require a separate, species-specific aquarium.

*Important Tip about Bettas:* Male Bettas (Siamese fighting fish) should NEVER be kept together. They will fight to the death. They can be kept with very peaceful, non-veil-tailed, fast-swimming fish that they will not mistake for rivals.

**Conclusion:** Always research the adult size of the fish and its natural behavior. A fish that looks cute in the store may become a predator or a source of constant stress for the other inhabitants.
